items.title: 5.2.1 Transform the General Linear Equation to Standard Forms

source_refs.note: Book p. 143-145: 5.2.1 Theorem 2, (i)-(vi) six standard forms with normal-form proof; Example 6; Challenge! box

blocks.text: Theorem 2: To transform the equation \(ax + by + c = 0\) in the standard forms.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why transform at all? Each standard form shows one property of the line at a glance: slope-intercept shows the slope and y-intercept; intercept form shows where the line cuts the axes; normal form shows the distance from the origin. The method in every part is the same: rearrange \(ax + by + c = 0\) until it looks exactly like the required form, then read off the constants.
(i) Slope-Intercept Form

We have
\[ax + by + c = 0\]
or
\[by = -ax - c\]
or
\[y = -\dfrac{a}{b}x - \dfrac{c}{b} = mx + k\]
(where \(b \neq 0\)), where
\[m = -\dfrac{a}{b}, \quad k = -\dfrac{c}{b}\]
(ii) Point-Slope Form

We note from above that slope of the line \(ax + by + c = 0\) is \(-\frac{a}{b}\) and y-intercept is \(-\frac{c}{b}\). So, the point \((-\frac{c}{a}, 0)\) lies on the line.
Equation of the straight line in point-slope form is
\[y - 0 = -\dfrac{a}{b}\left(x + \dfrac{c}{a}\right)\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Where does the point \((-\frac{c}{a}, 0)\) come from? Put \(y = 0\) in \(ax + by + c = 0\): \(ax + c = 0\), so \(x = -\frac{c}{a}\) (needs \(a \neq 0\)). This is the x-intercept point. Any point of the line would do; for example \((0, -\frac{c}{b})\) gives \(y + \frac{c}{b} = -\frac{a}{b}x\), which is the same line.
(iii) Symmetric Form

\[\dfrac{x - x_{1}}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{y - y_{1}}{\sin\theta}\]
\[= r \text{ (say)}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Meaning of the symmetric form: \(\theta\) is the inclination of the line and \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) a point on it. Moving a distance \(r\) along the line from \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) brings us to
\[x = x_{1} + r\cos\theta, \quad y = y_{1} + r\sin\theta\]
Solving each for \(r\) gives the two equal fractions. So \(r\) is the (signed) distance of \((x, y)\) from \((x_{1}, y_{1})\), and the pair \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) must point along the line, with \(\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta = m\).

\(m = \tan\theta = -\frac{a}{b}\), \(\sin\theta = \frac{a}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\), \(\cos\theta = \frac{b}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\)
A point on \(ax + by + c = 0\) is \((-\frac{c}{a}, 0)\).
So, equation of the straight line in symmetric form is:
\[\dfrac{x - \left(-\frac{c}{a}\right)}{\frac{b}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}} = r\]
\[\dfrac{y - 0}{\frac{a}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}} = r\]
Sign of the radical to be properly chosen.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book prints \(\sin\theta = \frac{a}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\), \(\cos\theta = \frac{b}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\) and then uses \(a\) as the denominator under \(y - 0\). These values give \(\tan\theta = \frac{a}{b}\), but the slope is \(m = \tan\theta = -\frac{a}{b}\). The sign of \(\sin\theta\) is wrong. The correct values (same sign of the radical in both) are
\[\cos\theta = \dfrac{b}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\]
\[\sin\theta = \dfrac{-a}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\]
so the symmetric form is
\[\dfrac{x + \frac{c}{a}}{\frac{b}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}} = \dfrac{y - 0}{\frac{-a}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}} = r\]
Test with \(x - y = 0\) (\(a = 1\), \(b = -1\), slope 1): the correct form gives direction \((\mp\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \mp\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\), slope 1; the printed form gives \((\mp\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\), slope \(-1\), a different line. Example 6 (vi) below uses the correct signs.
(iv) Two-Point Form

We choose two arbitrary points on \(ax + by + c = 0\). Two such points are \((-\frac{c}{a}, 0)\) and \((0, -\frac{c}{b})\). Equation of the straight line through these points is
\[\dfrac{y - 0}{0 + \frac{c}{b}} = \dfrac{x + \frac{c}{a}}{-\frac{c}{a} - 0}\]
or
\[y - 0 = \dfrac{\frac{c}{b}}{-\frac{c}{a}}\left(x + \dfrac{c}{a}\right)\]
or
\[y = -\dfrac{a}{b}\left(x + \dfrac{c}{a}\right)\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: This uses the two-point form \(\frac{y - y_{1}}{y_{1} - y_{2}} = \frac{x - x_{1}}{x_{1} - x_{2}}\) with \((x_{1}, y_{1}) = (-\frac{c}{a}, 0)\) and \((x_{2}, y_{2}) = (0, -\frac{c}{b})\). It needs \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) all non-zero: if \(c = 0\) both points are the origin, and one point cannot fix a line. Then choose another point, e.g. \(x = 1\), \(y = -\frac{a}{b}\).
(v) Two-Intercept Form

\[ax + by = -c\]
or
\[\dfrac{ax}{-c} + \dfrac{by}{-c} = 1\]
or
\[\dfrac{x}{\left(-\frac{c}{a}\right)} + \dfrac{y}{\left(-\frac{c}{b}\right)} = 1\]
where x-intercept \(= -\frac{c}{a}\), y-intercept \(= -\frac{c}{b}\), which is an equation of straight line in two-intercept form.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Two small steps: divide by \(-c\) so that the right side becomes 1 (needs \(c \neq 0\)); then write \(\frac{ax}{-c}\) as \(\frac{x}{-c/a}\), because dividing by \(\frac{-c}{a}\) is the same as multiplying by \(\frac{a}{-c}\).
(vi) Normal Form

The equation
\[ax + by + c = 0 \quad \ldots(i)\]
can be written in the normal form as:
\[\dfrac{ax + by}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}} = \dfrac{-c}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}} \quad \ldots(ii)\]
The sign of the radical to be such that the right hand side of (ii) is positive.

Proof: We know that an equation of a straight line in normal form is:
\[x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = p \quad \ldots(iii)\]
If (i) and (iii) are identical, we must have
\[\dfrac{a}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{b}{\sin\theta} = -\dfrac{c}{p}\]
i.e.
\[\dfrac{p}{-c} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{a} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{b}\]
\[= \dfrac{\sqrt{\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta}}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}} = \dfrac{1}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\]
Hence,
\[\cos\theta = \dfrac{a}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}, \quad \sin\theta = \dfrac{b}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\]
and
\[p = \dfrac{-c}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\]
Substituting values of \(\cos\theta\), \(\sin\theta\) and \(p\) in (iii), we have:
\[\dfrac{ax + by}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}} = \dfrac{-c}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\]
Thus (i) can be reduced to the form (ii) by dividing it by \(\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\). The sign of the radical to be chosen so that the right hand side of (ii) is positive.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why 'identical' means proportional: two equations of the same line can differ only by a constant factor, so the ratios of corresponding coefficients are equal. Write (i) as \(ax + by = -c\) and compare with \(x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = p\).
The step with \(\sqrt{\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta}\) uses the rule: if \(\frac{u}{a} = \frac{v}{b} = k\), then \(u = ka\), \(v = kb\), so \(\sqrt{u^{2} + v^{2}} = |k|\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}\), i.e. \(k = \frac{\sqrt{u^{2}+v^{2}}}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\).
Practical rule for the sign: if \(c < 0\) divide by \(+\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\); if \(c > 0\) divide by \(-\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\). Then \(p = \frac{|c|}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\) is the distance of the line from the origin.

blocks.title: Example 6
blocks.problem:
Transform the equation \(3x - 10y + 13 = 0\) into
(i) Slope-intercept form (ii) Two-intercept form (iii) Normal form (iv) Point-slope form (v) Two-point form (vi) Symmetric form
steps:
Given: \(3x - 10y + 13 = 0\), so \(a = 3\), \(b = -10\), \(c = 13\).
To find: the same line in six standard forms.
Method: follow Theorem 2 part by part. Most forms need the slope \(m = -\frac{a}{b} = \frac{3}{10}\) and one or two points on the line, so we find these as we go.

(i) Slope-intercept form
\[3x - 10y + 13 = 0\]
\[10y = 3x + 13\]
\[y = \dfrac{3}{10}x + \dfrac{13}{10}\]
where \(m = \frac{3}{10}\), \(c = \frac{13}{10}\).
Why: we keep the \(y\)-term alone on one side and divide by its coefficient 10.

(ii) Two-intercept form
\[3x - 10y = -13\]
\[\dfrac{3x}{-13} + \dfrac{10}{13}y = 1\]
\[\dfrac{x}{-\frac{13}{3}} + \dfrac{y}{\frac{13}{10}} = 1\]
Why: the right-hand side must be 1, so we divide by \(-13\); then each coefficient is moved to the denominator of the denominator. The intercepts are \(-\frac{13}{3}\) and \(\frac{13}{10}\).

(iii) Normal form: divide by the radical
\[3x - 10y = -13\]
Dividing both sides by
\[\pm\sqrt{(3)^{2} + (-10)^{2}} = \pm\sqrt{109}\]
Since R.H.S is to be positive, we have to take negative sign.
Why: in the normal form the right side is \(p\), a distance, so it cannot be negative. The R.H.S. is \(-13\); dividing by \(-\sqrt{109}\) makes it \(+\frac{13}{\sqrt{109}}\).

(iii) Normal form: result
Hence,
\[-\dfrac{3x}{\sqrt{109}} + \dfrac{10y}{\sqrt{109}} = \dfrac{13}{\sqrt{109}}\]
is the normal form of the given equation.
Why: now \(\cos\theta = -\frac{3}{\sqrt{109}}\), \(\sin\theta = \frac{10}{\sqrt{109}}\) (their squares add to 1) and \(p = \frac{13}{\sqrt{109}} \approx 1.245\). As \(\cos\theta < 0\), \(\sin\theta > 0\), \(\theta \approx 106.7^\circ\) (second quadrant).

(iv) Point-slope form
A point on the line is \((-\frac{13}{3}, 0)\) and its slope is \(\frac{3}{10}\).
Equation of line in point slope-form is:
\[y - 0 = \dfrac{3}{10}\left(x + \dfrac{13}{3}\right)\]
Why: putting \(y = 0\) in the equation gives \(3x + 13 = 0\), \(x = -\frac{13}{3}\); the slope comes from part (i).

(v) Two-point form
We take any two points \((-\frac{13}{3}, 0)\) and \((0, \frac{13}{10})\) on the line.
So, equation of the line in two-point form is:
\[\dfrac{y - 0}{\frac{13}{10} - 0} = \dfrac{x + \frac{13}{3}}{0 + \frac{13}{3}}\]
Why: the two intercept points are the easiest points to find (put \(y = 0\), then \(x = 0\)).

(vi) Symmetric form: find the direction
We have
\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{10} = m\]
\[\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{109}}, \quad \cos\theta = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{109}}\]
and a point on the line is \((-\frac{13}{3}, 0)\).
Why: here \(\theta\) is the inclination of the line. A right triangle with legs 10 (adjacent) and 3 (opposite) has hypotenuse \(\sqrt{100 + 9} = \sqrt{109}\). Since \(m > 0\), we take \(\theta\) acute, so both are positive.

(vi) Symmetric form: result
Equation of the line in symmetric form is:
\[\dfrac{x + \frac{13}{3}}{\frac{10}{\sqrt{109}}} = \dfrac{y - 0}{\frac{3}{\sqrt{109}}}\]
\[= r \text{ (say)}\]
Why: the form is \(\frac{x - x_{1}}{\cos\theta} = \frac{y - y_{1}}{\sin\theta} = r\) with \((x_{1}, y_{1}) = (-\frac{13}{3}, 0)\).

Check:
(ii): \(-\frac{3x}{13} + \frac{10y}{13} = 1\); multiply by 13: \(-3x + 10y = 13\), the given line.
(v) and (vi): cross-multiplying (vi) gives \(3(x + \frac{13}{3}) = 10y\), that is \(3x - 10y + 13 = 0\). Each form returns the given equation.

blocks.title: Challenge!
blocks.text: Transform the equation \(2x + 5y - 10 = 0\) into slope-intercept form, two-intercept form, normal form, point-slope form, two-point form and symmetric form.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Try the Challenge yourself first, then compare (our answers):
Slope-intercept: \(y = -\frac{2}{5}x + 2\).
Two-intercept: \(\frac{x}{5} + \frac{y}{2} = 1\).
Normal (here \(c = -10 < 0\), so divide by \(+\sqrt{29}\)): \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}}x + \frac{5}{\sqrt{29}}y = \frac{10}{\sqrt{29}}\).
Point-slope (point \((5, 0)\)): \(y - 0 = -\frac{2}{5}(x - 5)\).
Two-point (points \((5, 0)\), \((0, 2)\)): \(\frac{y - 0}{2 - 0} = \frac{x - 5}{0 - 5}\).
Symmetric (\(\cos\theta = \frac{5}{\sqrt{29}}\), \(\sin\theta = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}}\)): \(\frac{x - 5}{5/\sqrt{29}} = \frac{y - 0}{-2/\sqrt{29}} = r\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Slope \(m = -\frac{a}{b}\); x-intercept \(-\frac{c}{a}\); y-intercept \(-\frac{c}{b}\). Almost every form is built from these three numbers.
2. Intercept form: make the right side 1 by dividing by \(-c\).
3. Normal form: divide by \(\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\), sign chosen so that the right side is positive.
4. Symmetric form: \(\cos\theta\), \(\sin\theta\) must give \(\tan\theta = m\); use \(\cos\theta = \frac{b}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\), \(\sin\theta = \frac{-a}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\).
5. Check any form by simplifying it back to \(ax + by + c = 0\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. In the normal form, choosing the sign of the radical so that the left side looks nice; the rule is: right side positive.
2. Forgetting the minus sign of an intercept: for \(3x - 10y + 13 = 0\) the x-intercept is \(-\frac{13}{3}\).
3. Copying the book's \(\sin\theta = \frac{a}{\pm\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\) into the symmetric form: the direction then has slope \(\frac{a}{b}\), the wrong sign.
4. Using the intercept points in the two-point form when \(c = 0\) (both are the origin).
